Title: MOCA: A Transformer-based Modular Causal Inference Framework with One-way Cross-attention and Cutting Feedback
Text:
MOCA: A Transformer-based Modular Causal Inference Framework
with One-way Cross-attention and Cutting Feedback
Lei Wang
Department of Biostatistics and Informatics
Colorado School of Public Health

Abstract
Causal effect estimation from observational data requires careful adjustment for confounding.
Classical estimators such as inverse probability weighting and augmented inverse probability
weighting are effective under favorable model specification, but may become unstable when
treatment assignment and outcome mechanisms are complex, non-linear and high-dimensional.
Machine learning and representation-learning approaches improve flexibility, yet joint training
can allow outcome-related information to influence treatment-side representations, which is unde-
sirable from a causal perspective. We propose MOCA (Modular One-way Causal Attention), a
transformer-based framework that separates treatment and outcome modeling through modular
design, and makes confounder adjustments with a one-way attention process. A cutting-feedback
strategy implemented with gradient detachment further prevents outcome loss from updating
the treatment module. This design preserves directional information flow while retaining the
representation power of transformer architectures for causal inference. Across multiple simulated
scenarios, including linear, nonlinear, heavy-tailed, hidden-confounding, and high-dimensional
settings, MOCA showed competitive or improved performance relative to IPW, AIPW, X-learner,
TARNet, and DragonNet. We further illustrate the method on Infant Health and Development
Program dataset and Dehejia–Wahba dataset for real world benchmarks. These results suggest
that modular attention with one-way information flow provides a promising and interpretable
direction for causal inference with modern deep learning models.
Keywords: causal inference; transformer; cross-attention; modular learning; treatment effect
estimation; cutting feedback
1
Introduction
In observational studies, treatment assignment is typically not randomized, leading to the pres-
ence of confounders that affect both treatment assignment and outcomes. Many modern causal
methodologies are built on the Rubin potential outcomes framework [Rubin, 2005]. A central
quantity of interest is the average treatment effect (ATE). Classical approaches can perform well
when the models are correctly specified. Propensity score methods like inverse probability weighting
(IPW) [Robins et al., 2000] and doubly robust estimators such as augmented inverse probability
weighting (AIPW) [Bang and Robins, 2005] are widely used approaches for confounding adjustment.

However, parametric causal estimators often rely on restrictive assumptions, and cannot capture
complex patterns such as nonlinear effects, or high-dimensional covariates. To address these limi-
tations and give conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates, machine learning-based
approaches, such as the T-learner and X-learner have been introduced [Künzel et al., 2019]. Besides,
representation-learning approaches such as TARNet [Johansson et al., 2016] and DragonNet [Shi
et al., 2019] have embedded the problem of causal inference within a deep learning framework
consisting of representation learning paired with two potential outcome heads.
Yet joint representation learning may allow for outcome information to affect treatment repre-
sentations, which is undesired in causal estimation. To address these challenges, we draw inspiration
from recent advances in transformer architectures and cross-attention mechanisms with a modular
framework. Transformers [Vaswani et al., 2017] have demonstrated remarkable ability to capture
complex dependent structures through attention-based representation learning, while cross-attention
provides a natural mechanism for directional information transfer between modules. Building on
these ideas, we propose a modular causal modeling framework in this article.
In our framework, the treatment branch is designed to learn propensity-related representations,
while the outcome branch receives treatment-side information only through one-way cross-attention.
This two-step design reflects the causal role of treatment modeling as an adjustment mechanism
for confounding. We also incorporate a cutting-feedback strategy through gradient detachment,
preventing the outcome loss from propagating backward to affect the treatment module.
Our proposed method, MOCA (Modular One-way Causal Attention), preserves treatment
modeling independence while still allowing the outcome module to adapt to complex response surfaces.
In this way, the framework retains modern machine learning advantages while maintaining the
structural requirements of causal inference and supporting interpretable treatment effect estimation.

Problem Setup and Causal Estimand
We consider an observational dataset consisting of n independent units: {(Xi, Ti, Yi)}n
i=1 , where
Xi ∈Rp denotes the observed covariates, Ti ∈{0, 1} is the binary treatment indicator, and Yi is
the observed outcome. Under the potential outcomes framework, each unit i has two potential
outcomes, Yi(0) and Yi(1), corresponding to the outcomes that would be observed under control
and treatment [Rubin, 2005]. The following assumptions are made.
1. Consistency: the observed outcome equals the corresponding potential outcome under the
treatment received: Yi = Yi (Ti), implying no other version of treatment;
2. Ignorability (unconfoundedness): (Yi(0), Yi(1))⊥Ti | Xi. That is, conditional on the observed
covariates, treatment assignment is independent of the potential outcomes, which implies no
unobserved confounding;
3. Positivity: 0 < P (Ti = 1 | Xi = x) < 1 for all x in the support of X, which ensures that each
covariate profile has a positive probability of receiving either treatment level.
For a unit i with covariate vector Xi = xi, a natural goal is to evaluate its individual level
treatment effect (ITE), τi := Yi(1) −Yi(0). However, τi is fundamentally unobservable, since for
each unit we only observe one potential outcome.
We instead focus on the conditional average treatment effect (CATE), τ(x) := E{Y (1) −Y (0) |
X = x}. Although τ(x) is a population-level quantity, it serves as the optimal target for individual-
level prediction. In particular, let ˆτ(Xi) denote an estimator of τi. The mean squared error (MSE)

3.5
Modularization and Cutting Feedback Rules
Cutting feedback originates from modular Bayesian analysis, where unwanted reverse feedback is
removed during posterior updating [Frazier and Nott, 2025]. In our work, we mimic this principle
through a two-step estimation procedure. There are four rules [Liu and Goudie, 2025] used here to
ensure a meaningful modular mechanism.
3.5.1
Rule 1: Self-contained modules
This rule requires the model to be decomposed into distinct modules, where each module is
self-contained; that is, internally coherent and functionally separable from the rest of the system
(Figure 2). We have introduced two modules: a treatment module and an outcome module. Formally,
we write ΨT = (X, T; θS,T , θL,T ), ΨY = (X, T, Y ; θS,Y , θL,Y ). The treatment module produces an
intermediate representation H(T), which acts as frozen information passed to the downstream
outcome module. The overlap between the two modules is ΨT∩Y = {X, T; H(T)}. Since {X, T}
is the observed dataset and H(T) is the frozen representative information, each module remains
self-contained in the sense that it is defined by its own data inputs and corresponding parameters.
3.5.2
Rule 2: Module ordering
The direction of information flow is explicitly defined from the treatment module to the outcome
module. In other words, the treatment module is treated as the parent module, and the outcome
module is treated as the child module. Hence, our method satisfies Rule 2 by explicitly imposing
the directed modular order ΨT ≺ΨY .
3.5.3
Rule 3: Cutting feedback
This rule states that inference for the parent module should be based only on its own module. In our
work, we implement this idea through stop-gradient. Specifically, the outcome model is written as

3.5.4
Rule 4: A cut-style downstream update
In modular Bayesian analysis, this rule refers to posterior updating under a cut distribution. In our
machine learning framework, we instead propose a cut-style downstream update for the parameters

in the outcome module. Step 1 learns the treatment module, and Step 2 learns the outcome module
conditional on the treatment representation. This is directly analogous to the logic of cut inference in
modular Bayesian analysis: pcut(θT , θY | data) = p(θT | treatment data) · p(θY | θT , outcome data).

4.2
Machine Learning Based Causal Effect Estimation
Meta-learning approaches adapt supervised learning algorithms to estimate treatment effects. The
T-learner fits two separate outcome models, using the control and treated samples respectively, and
estimates the treatment effect by bτ(x) = bµ1(x) −bµ0(x).
This approach is simple and flexible, but may suffer when one treatment group has limited sample
size. The X-learner improves upon the T-learner by first imputing pseudo-treatment effects and then
learning treatment effect functions separately in each group, often achieving better performance
under treatment imbalance [Künzel et al., 2019]. In our analysis, we will compare to X-learner since
it considers the treatment adjustments.
Representation learning methods for causal inference seek to learn latent covariate representations
that are useful for estimating both treatment assignment and potential outcomes. TARNet and
DragonNet are two examples.
Let Φ(X) denote a learned representation of the covariates. TARNet predicts the two potential
outcome surfaces through separate heads [Johansson et al., 2016]:
bµ0(X) = h0(Φ(X)), bµ1(X) = h1(Φ(X)).
The factual prediction is

4.3
Transformer for Tabular Data
Transformer and attention-based architectures have recently shown strong performance in tabular
modeling because they can flexibly capture nonlinear dependencies and higher-order feature interac-
tions [Wang et al., 2025]. Such flexibility is potentially valuable for causal inference, however, the
application of transformers in causal inference is still a new attempt. For example, utilizing Trans-
formers to capture complex, long-range dependencies among time-varying confounders [Melnychuk
et al., 2022].
Most existing causal models typically do not emphasize directional information flow between
treatment and outcome representations, nor do they explicitly implement cutting feedback to
prevent outcome-side gradients from updating treatment-side representations. These limitations
motivate architectures that preserve the representational power of attention while introducing
mechanism-aware structure.

5
Simulation Study
To comprehensively evaluate the performance of the proposed method, we conducted six simulation
studies under multiple data-generating mechanisms. Including MOCA with its one-way and two-way
version, there are 7 methods compared in the simulation. IPW and AIPW are well-established
methods in classical causal inference, and AIPW is especially attractive due to its doubly robust
property. X-learner represent machine-learning-based approaches that have shown competitive
performance in treatment effect estimation. TARNet and DragonNet are representation-learning
methods and provide important neural-network-based benchmarks for comparison.
All simulations and model training were conducted in Python (3.11.4). The proposed model was
implemented in PyTorch (version 2.5.1+cu121), with NumPy (version 2.4.3) and Pandas (3.0.1)
used for data generation and numerical computation. Random seeds with different seeds for different
samples were fixed to ensure reproducibility. We considered two sample-size settings: 100 and 1,000
observations in each of the training, validation, and test sets.
5.1
Simulation setting
The data generation mechanisms are based on a classical setting of potential outcomes.

6
Results
6.1
Simulation Results
The simulation results suggest that MOCA is competitive for ATE estimation across all considered
settings, and that the one-way attention version generally performs better than the two-way version
[Table 1]. This supports the overall effectiveness of MOCA and highlights the value of one-way
attention and cutting feedback.
Under nonlinear, t-distribution, and high-dimensional settings, MOCA outperform traditional
methods such as IPW and AIPW with less outliers [Figure 3-4]. IPW and AIPW may have the
estimated propensity scores become extremely large or small [Rosenbaum and Rubin, 1983], leading
to unstable weights, increased bias, more outliers, and ultimately larger RMSE [Li et al., 2019]. In
these scenarios, MOCA is not only competitive with other machine learning approaches, but also
clearly improves upon traditional estimators.
Under violations of ignorabillity through the presence of hidden confounders, MOCA also shows
advantages when the sample size is small. In particular, its bias is generally smaller than that of
competing methods, and the one-way version again performs better than the two-way version. This
suggests that when the model is misspecified and information is incomplete, it is important to prevent
mutual contamination between the treatment module and the outcome module. However, when the
sample size increases to 1000, none of the methods can estimate the ATE well [Table S1, Figure
S1-S2]. Therefore, although MOCA shows some robustness to ignorability violation in small samples,
valid estimation still fundamentally relies on identifiable assumptions being satisfied [VanderWeele
and Arah, 2011].
For CATE estimation, this is one of the main advantages of machine learning based approaches
[Table S2-S3, Figure S3-S4]. Because MOCA, X-learner, TARNet, and DragonNet can all produce
individual-level predictions of the potential outcomes, it is natural to further assess their ability to
estimate CATE. Overall, MOCA is effective for CATE estimation in most scenarios.
TARNet, and DragonNet, which rely on learned representations, perform worse than the meta-
learning frameworks X-learner under heavy-tailed t-distributed data. Shared representations and
trained with squared-error loss can be less stable under heavy-tailed outcomes [Fan et al., 2021].
MOCA, on the other hand, still provided a relatively comparable result.
Overall, MOCA performs better than traditional methods such as IPW and AIPW under
nonlinear, high-dimensional, t-distributed, and even hidden-confounding settings, while remaining
competitive with other machine learning based methods. At the same time, the use of one-way
attention and cutting feedback helps reduce potential information pollution and preserves the
methodological rationale of the model within the causal inference framework.
6.2
Real Data Results
Two open-sourced real datasets are used here [Table 2]. We estimated uncertainty for MOCA by
repeatedly fitting the model and combining the resulting ATE estimates using a Rubin-style pooling
rule [Barnard and Rubin, 1999]. IHDP refers to the Infant Health and Development Program
dataset, which comes from a randomized experiment conducted between 1985 and 1988 to study
the effect of home-based intervention on infants’ cognitive test scores [Louizos et al., 2017]. There
are 747 observations with 608 controls and 139 treatments. This version contains the treatment
indicator, the observed outcome yfactual, the counterfactual outcome ycfactual, the mean potential
outcomes under control and treatment (µ0 and µ1), and 25 covariates. Among these, X1–X6 are
continuous variables, while X7–X25 are binary variables. A counterfactual outcome included in
this dataset, so that we can show the ATE bias directly. The IHDP results show that MOCA has
11


the smallest ATE bias of 0.006. We have a pooling estimated ATE of 3.991 and a 95% confidence
interval of (3.69, 4.29).
DW refers to the Dehejia–Wahba dataset, which is a subset of the Lalonde data [Dehejia and
Wahba, 1999]. It contains 445 observations with 185 treatments and 260 controls. Typically,
we expected ATE is a positive number, and the doubly robust method AIPW can be a good
reference [Iacus et al., 2019]. The variables include the treatment indicator treated, age, education,
race, marital status, no-degree status, earnings in 1974 and 1975, post-treatment earnings in 1978,
and unemployment indicators u74 and u75. Among these, re78 is usually treated as the post-
treatment outcome. However, this dataset does not have a truth for reference. In this case, we will
report only the ATE instead. The ATE based on doubly robust method AIPW is 784.214 with a
95% confidence interval of (-1746.59, 3315.02), which is a potential reference for other methods.
MOCA pooling estimates ATE to be 672.201 and a 95% confidence interval of (-388.15, 1732.55),
which is closest to the AIPW method.
7
Discussion
In conclusion, this paper introduces a modular causal transformer framework that combines represen-
tation learning, one-way cross-attention, and cutting feedback for treatment effect estimation. The
proposed design aims to preserve the usefulness of treatment information for confounding adjustment
while avoiding undesirable reverse influence from outcome learning to treatment representation.
Empirical results show that this framework can provide competitive and often improved performance,
particularly in settings with nonlinear covariate effects, treatment effect heterogeneity, and complex
dependency structures.
At the same time, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, although the proposed
model showed favorable empirical performance, it remains more computationally intensive than
conventional estimators such as IPW, AIPW. Transformer-based architectures require tuning of
multiple hyperparameters and may be sensitive to optimization settings, sample size, and training
stability.
In relatively simple settings, the added complexity of the model may not translate
into substantial improvement over simpler approaches. Richer architectures can better capture
complex structure, but may also overfit or underperform when the true mechanism is simple or
when the available sample size is limited [Hastie et al., 2009]. Second, the validity of the MOCA
still relies on standard identification assumptions such as consistency, ignorability, and positivity.
The model cannot fully correct for hidden confounding when important variables are entirely
unobserved. Third, although the one-way modular design helps reduce feedback contamination, it
still relies on the correctness of treatment module. In addition, the hard cutting of feedback, while
conceptually attractive for protecting the treatment mechanism, may be overly restrictive in some
settings [Carmona and Nicholls, 2020]. This suggests that the optimal degree of modularization
may vary across applications. In addition, future work could explore methods that combine the
proposed architecture with sensitivity analysis or proxy-variable strategies to better address hidden
confounding.

Abstract: Causal effect estimation from observational data requires careful adjustment for confounding. Classical estimators such as inverse probability weighting and augmented inverse probability weighting are effective under favorable model specification, but may become unstable when treatment assignment and outcome mechanisms are complex, non-linear and high-dimensional. Machine learning and representation-learning approaches improve flexibility, yet joint training can allow outcome-related information to influence treatment-side representations, which is unde- sirable from a causal perspective. We propose MOCA (Modular One-way Causal Attention), a transformer-based framework that separates treatment and outcome modeling through modular design, and makes confounder adjustments with a one-way attention process. A cutting-feedback strategy implemented with gradient detachment further prevents outcome loss from updating the treatment module. This design preserves directional information flow while retaining the representation power of transformer architectures for causal inference. Across multiple simulated scenarios, including linear, nonlinear, heavy-tailed, hidden-confounding, and high-dimensional settings, MOCA showed competitive or improved performance relative to IPW, AIPW, X-learner, TARNet, and DragonNet. We further illustrate the method on Infant Health and Development Program dataset and Dehejia–Wahba dataset for real world benchmarks. These results suggest that modular attention with one-way information flow provides a promising and interpretable direction for causal inference with modern deep learning models.
